item.title: U.S. futures mostly higher as Wall Street digests earnings from SpaceX, Netflix
item.description: U.S. futures are higher as Wall Street digests the latest round of earnings reports while oil prices tick higher.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: U.S. futures are higher as Wall Street digests the latest round of earnings reports while oil prices tick higher. Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent on Wednesday, while those for the Nasdaq climbed 0.4 per cent. Futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average were nearly flat. Big expectations for earnings growth have pushed the U.S. stock market to record highs despite high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. SpaceX’s stock jumped more than eight per cent before the market open Wednesday as the Elon Musk-led company reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected as its satellite communications and artificial intelligence businesses boomed. Musk said SpaceX and Tesla have formed “special committees” to discuss a merger of the two companies, though he played down the chances of an imminent deal. Shares of Netflix dropped more than six per cent in premarket trading as the streaming company lowered its ad sales guidance on Tuesday, prompting worries about slowing revenue growth. Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street expectations. Investors will be waiting for earnings from companies such as Meta and Tesla on Wednesday. Oil prices have soared due to the Iran war and fuel costs have followed with the risks of transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 1.3 per cent to US$110.21 per barrel Wednesday. A day earlier it rose to nearly $112, approaching its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February. Brent’s price has been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 per barrel this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry will return to normal. U.S. benchmark crude rose 1.6 per cent to $99.40 per barrel. In Europe, Germany’s DAX climbed 0.7 per cent to 25,489.81 and the CAC 40 in Paris added 0.6 per cent to 7,888.32. Britain’s FTSE 100 edged 0.1 per cent higher, to 10,741.70. Asian markets were mixed. The U.S. dollar slipped to 158.08 Japanese yen from 158.17 yen. The euro fell to $1.1233 from $1.1239. By Elaine Kurtenbach and Michelle Chapman

item.title: Anthropic logged net loss of over US$80 billion in first half of 2026
item.description: Anthropic’s net loss widened sharply to US$80.7 billion in the first half of this year, in large part due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into shares of the AI startup, according to a ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Anthropic’s net loss widened sharply to US$80.7 billion in the first half of this year, in large part due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into shares of the AI startup, according to a draft prospectus for a planned initial public offering that was reviewed by Reuters. The San Francisco-based company is expected to go public in November and some investors are now weighing a lower valuation of around $1.5 trillion following its latest financial disclosures, Reuters reported last week. Its first-half loss, widening from a loss of $13 billion a year earlier, included a $72 billion accounting charge reflecting an increase in the estimated value of bonds that could eventually convert into Anthropic shares, rather than cash costs tied to its operations, the document said. The disclosures underscore the hefty costs of the AI race even as investors give greater scrutiny to whether the vast sums being poured into chips and data centers will generate sufficient returns. Anthropic has committed to spending at least $518 billion over a decade on cloud services, computing and infrastructure. The company spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half, up from $2.3 billion a year earlier, the S-1 document showed. Anthropic did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Financing costs At an investor meeting on October 14, Anthropic told prospective IPO investors that its third-quarter revenue jumped 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. While the figures eased some concerns about the enormous costs of developing AI systems, some investors were disappointed by the slowing sequential growth rate. Revenue had more than doubled from the first quarter to $11.6 billion in the second quarter. A cooler reception for Anthropic’s IPO could weigh on the wider AI market, whose near-term prospects investors see as hinging largely on the share sale’s success, ahead of rival OpenAI’s potential listing next year. Reuters reported in September that Anthropic posted a net loss of $42 billion in 2025, with most of that stemming from a similar accounting charge. As Anthropic’s valuation climbed, the estimated fair value of those notes tripled year over year. Excluding the charge, Anthropic posted an operating loss of about $8.1 billion on $4.6 billion of revenue in 2025. The company has benefited from the popularity of Claude Code, its coding assistant that developers use to write software and build apps. Reporting by Echo Wang, Aditya Soni, Jaspreet Singh and Rajveer Singh Pardesi in Bengaluru; Editing by Sahal Muhammed, Miyoung Kim and Thomas Derpinghaus, Reuters

item.title: APEC finance ministers warn persistent global imbalances risk growth and stability
item.description: Senior Pacific Rim finance officials say global economic imbalances are bringing persistent risks and have pledged to improve cooperation and communication.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: HONG KONG — Senior Pacific Rim finance officials say global economic imbalances are bringing persistent risks and have pledged to improve co-operation and communication. In a joint statement after two days of meetings in Hong Kong, the finance leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum emphasized Wednesday that rebalancing of trade is their common interest. However, they did not elaborate on specific measures to be taken. The meetings, in preparation for an APEC summit next month in the nearby Chinese city of Shenzhen, come at a time when global policymakers are highlighting the need to rebalance trade with China. Its trade surplus this year is expected to exceed 2025’s record US$1.2 trillion. The officials also pointed to risks from geopolitical tensions and vulnerable supply chains. “We note that global imbalances have persisted, creating risks to growth and stability,” the statement said. APEC’s 21 member economies include China, the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Canada and Australia, among other Pacific Rim countries. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen. Chinese finance minister Lan Fo’an, as chair of the APEC finance ministers’ meeting, said members had agreed to improve coordination of economic policies to address risks and challenges. China’s customs agency said last week that the country’s trade with other APEC economies rose nearly 24 per cent in the first three quarters of this year from a year earlier, driven by surging exports of high-tech products including electric vehicles and lithium-ion batteries. Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

item.title: ‘We’re going to take care of Bombardier’: Trump backs down on threat against Canadian jet maker
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take “good care” of the company’s workers in Kansas.
item.dc:creator: Graham Richardson
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA – U.S. President Donald Trump appears to be backing away from his threat to shut Canadian aerospace giant Bombardier out of the U.S. market, after learning about the company’s significant operations in Kansas. In September, Trump threatened to block sales of Bombardier jets in the United States amid a growing trade dispute with Canada. “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 7. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’” But while visiting Kansas on Monday, Trump struck a dramatically different tone after learning about Bombardier’s operations in Wichita, where the company employs about 1,500 people. “We’re going to take care of Bombardier,” Trump told 12 News in Kansas. He repeated the sentiment on stage at a rally later in the day. “I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away … I’ll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company,” Trump said. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So, we’ll take care of those people and the jobs.” Dominic LeBlanc, the federal minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, has argued for months that Bombardier is deeply embedded in the American economy. “Bombardier has many hundreds and thousands of employees in the United States and has had for a long time. I had seen a number of legislators in the United States, including Republicans, express concerns this summer when President Trump had made those comments about Bombardier,” said Leblanc. Trump was in Kansas to campaign for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is locked in an unusually competitive re-election fight against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Kansas has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, but polls have shown a close race this year. Trump’s September threat against Bombardier had become a political issue in Kansas because of the company’s 1,500 jobs in Wichita. Marshall was among the Kansas lawmakers who contacted the White House after Trump threatened to block Bombardier from the U.S. market. Trump specifically cited Marshall’s involvement when he told local television Monday that his administration would “take care of Bombardier.” Bombardier employs about 3,500 people across the United States, with more than 40 per cent of those jobs in Wichita. The company last week announced a US$50-million investment in Wichita, home to its U.S. and defence headquarters. “We’re going to find a deal with the United States at some point that’s in the interest of the entire Canadian economy,” said Leblanc.
